Starsim is built for infectious diseases, but its machinery for agents is general: a population of agents, each with properties kept as arrays over all of them; modules that change those properties at each step; results recorded over time; and random numbers drawn so that runs can be repeated and compared. A [module written as code](../user_guide/building_modules.qmd) can hold any property of people and any rule for changing it, so Starsim can run agent-based models with no disease at all. This page shows two classic ones: a model of wealth, from economics, and a model of flocking birds, from computer graphics.

Not every model of something other than an infection needs code. States and transitions describe any process in which people move between categories at given rates (smoking, use of contraception, stages of a chronic disease, employment), and a declared model of such a process runs under every solver, with the same interventions as a disease: see [Diseases](../user_guide/building_diseases.qmd). Some models track things that are not people at all, such as bacteria in water or a population of mosquitoes, as states with `people=False` in the same model as the people (see [Cholera with a water reservoir](cholera.qmd)).

## Wealth

This is the "wealth model" of the [Mesa](https://mesa.readthedocs.io/latest/tutorials/0_first_model.html) tutorial: each person starts with one unit of wealth, and gives one unit at a time to someone chosen at random. Though the rule is fair, wealth ends up very unequal. Here each person who has any gives with a chance of 1 in 10 at each step, so that inequality builds up over steps rather than all in the first.

| Parameter | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| People | 1,000 | |
| Starting wealth | 1 unit | The same for everyone |
| Giving | 1 unit | With a chance of 0.1 a step, from each person who has any, to someone chosen at random |
| Steps | 100 | |

Each person's wealth is a state, and who gives and to whom are drawn from Starsim distributions, so that runs can be repeated and compared (see [Random numbers](../user_guide/mechanics_random.qmd)). The Gini coefficient (0 if everyone has the same, near 1 if one person has everything) is a result:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import sciris as sc
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import starsim as ss

class Wealth(ss.Module):
    """ Each person starts with 1 unit of wealth; each step, a tenth of those with any give 1 unit to someone chosen at random """

    p_give    = ss.par(ss.bernoulli(p=0.1)) # The chance that a person who has any wealth gives a unit in a step
    recipient = ss.par(ss.randint(low=0, high=lambda self, sim, uids: len(sim.people))) # Whom each giver gives to: a position, the same as a UID only since nobody is born or dies here
    wealth    = ss.FloatArr(default=1.0, label='Wealth')

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(
            ss.Result('gini', label='Gini coefficient', kind='ratio'),
        )
        return

    def step(self):
        givers = self.pars.p_give.filter((self.wealth > 0).uids)
        recipients = self.pars.recipient.rvs(givers)
        self.wealth[givers] = self.wealth[givers] - 1
        self.wealth[:] = self.wealth + np.bincount(recipients, minlength=len(self.wealth)) # Each recipient gets 1 unit for each giver who chose them
        return

    def record_states(self): # The state at the start of each step
        super().record_states()
        w = np.sort(self.wealth.values)
        n = len(w)
        self.results.gini[self.ti] = np.sum((2*np.arange(1, n+1) - n - 1)*w)/(n*w.sum())
        return
```

## R

```r
library(starsim)
library(reticulate) # For py_to_r(), which gives an R value

Wealth <- Class("Wealth", ss$Module, # Each person starts with 1 unit of wealth; each step, a tenth of those with any give 1 unit to someone chosen at random
  p_give    = par(ss$bernoulli(p = 0.1)), # The chance that a person who has any wealth gives a unit in a step
  recipient = par(ss$randint(low = 0, high = py_func(function(self, sim, uids) length(sim$people)))), # Whom each giver gives to: a position, the same as a UID only since nobody is born or dies here
  wealth    = ss$FloatArr(default = 1.0, label = "Wealth"),

  init_results = function(self) {
    ss$Module$init_results(self)
    self$define_results(ss$Result("gini", label = "Gini coefficient", kind = "ratio"))
  },

  step = function(self) {
    givers <- self$pars$p_give$filter((self$wealth > 0)$uids)
    recipients <- py_to_r(self$pars$recipient$rvs(givers))
    self$wealth[givers] <- self$wealth[givers] - 1
    self$wealth[] <- self$wealth + tabulate(recipients + 1, nbins = length(self$wealth)) # Each recipient gets 1 unit for each giver who chose them (UIDs count from 0)
  },

  record_states = function(self) { # The state at the start of each step
    ss$Module$record_states(self)
    w <- sort(py_to_r(self$wealth$values))
    n <- length(w)
    self$results$gini[self$ti] <- sum((2 * seq_len(n) - n - 1) * w) / (n * sum(w))
  }
)
```
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
sim = ss.Sim(Wealth(), n_agents=1000, stop=100) # 100 steps
sim.run()
sim.results.wealth.gini.plot()
```

## R

```r
sim <- Sim(Wealth(), n_agents = 1000, stop = 100) # 100 steps
sim$run()
sim$results$wealth$gini$plot()
```
:::

Inequality rises over the first 10 or so steps, and then stays high, with a Gini coefficient of about 0.65, close to that of the most unequal countries. The final distribution has many people with nothing and a few with several units:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
wealth = sim.people.wealth.wealth
plt.figure()
plt.hist(wealth.values, bins=np.arange(wealth.max() + 2) - 0.5)
plt.xlabel('Wealth')
plt.ylabel('Number of people')
plt.show()
```

## R

```r
wealth <- sim$people$wealth$wealth$values
hist(wealth, breaks = seq(-0.5, max(wealth) + 0.5), xlab = "Wealth", ylab = "Number of people", main = "")
```
:::

Compared with Mesa, where each agent is an object with its own `step()`, Starsim keeps each property as one array over all people, so a rule is applied to everyone at once, as operations on arrays.

## Flocking

Boids are the classic model of flocking, in which each bird follows three simple rules about the birds it can see: **alignment** (steer towards their average heading), **cohesion** (steer towards their center), and **separation** (steer away from any that are too close). No bird leads, and nobody tells the flock where to go, but flocks form and fly together.

| Parameter | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Boids | 200 | |
| Sight | 0.1 | How far a boid can see, in a world that is a unit square |
| Too close | 0.03 | The distance within which a boid steers away |
| Alignment, cohesion, separation | 0.1, 0.005, 3 × 10⁻⁵ | How strongly each rule steers |
| Speed | 0.005 to 0.01 | The minimum and maximum distance moved in a step |
| Steps | 200 | |

In Starsim, each boid's position (`x`, `y`) and velocity (`vx`, `vy`) are states, starting at random. The world is a unit square whose edges wrap around, so a boid leaving on the right comes back on the left. At each step, the module works out the offset from every boid to every other (the short way round), applies the three rules to all the boids at once, keeps each boid's speed between a minimum and a maximum, and moves them. How well the flock is aligned is a result: for each boid, the length of the average heading of those it can see (itself included), averaged over all boids, which is 1 when each moves with its neighbors and close to 0 when their headings are random:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
class Boids(ss.Module):
    """ Flocking: each boid steers towards the heading and center of the boids it can see, and away from those too close """

    radius     = ss.par(0.1)    # How far a boid can see (the world is a unit square)
    too_close  = ss.par(0.03)   # How close is too close
    alignment  = ss.par(0.1)    # How strongly a boid steers towards its neighbors' heading
    cohesion   = ss.par(0.005)  # ... towards its neighbors' center
    separation = ss.par(3e-5)   # ... away from those too close
    speed      = ss.par([0.005, 0.01]) # The minimum and maximum distance moved in a step
    x  = ss.FloatArr(default=ss.random(), label='Position (x)')
    y  = ss.FloatArr(default=ss.random(), label='Position (y)')
    vx = ss.FloatArr(default=ss.uniform(-0.01, 0.01), label='Velocity (x)')
    vy = ss.FloatArr(default=ss.uniform(-0.01, 0.01), label='Velocity (y)')

    def init_results(self):
        super().init_results()
        self.define_results(ss.Result('aligned', label='Alignment with neighbors', kind='ratio'))
        return

    def snapshot(self):
        """ A copy of the boids' positions and velocities """
        return sc.obj(x=self.x.copy(), y=self.y.copy(), vx=self.vx.copy(), vy=self.vy.copy())

    def offsets(self):
        """ The offsets from each boid to every other, the short way round the edges, and the distances """
        x, y = self.x.values, self.y.values
        dx = x[None, :] - x[:, None]
        dy = y[None, :] - y[:, None]
        dx -= np.round(dx)
        dy -= np.round(dy)
        return dx, dy, np.hypot(dx, dy)

    def step(self):
        p = self.pars
        vx, vy = self.vx.values, self.vy.values
        dx, dy, dist = self.offsets()
        np.fill_diagonal(dist, np.inf) # A boid is not its own neighbor
        near = dist < p.radius
        n_near = np.maximum(near.sum(axis=1), 1)
        close = dist < p.too_close

        # The three rules, for all the boids at once
        steer_x = p.alignment*(near @ vx / n_near - vx) + p.cohesion*(near*dx).sum(axis=1)/n_near - p.separation*(close*dx/dist**2).sum(axis=1)
        steer_y = p.alignment*(near @ vy / n_near - vy) + p.cohesion*(near*dy).sum(axis=1)/n_near - p.separation*(close*dy/dist**2).sum(axis=1)
        alone = ~near.any(axis=1) # A boid that sees nobody flies straight on
        vx = vx + np.where(alone, 0, steer_x)
        vy = vy + np.where(alone, 0, steer_y)

        # Keep the speed within limits, then move, wrapping around the edges
        speed = np.hypot(vx, vy)
        factor = np.clip(speed, *p.speed)/speed
        self.vx[:] = vx*factor
        self.vy[:] = vy*factor
        self.x[:] = (self.x + self.vx) % 1
        self.y[:] = (self.y + self.vy) % 1
        return

    def record_states(self): # The state at the start of each step
        super().record_states()
        speed = np.hypot(self.vx.values, self.vy.values)
        hx, hy = self.vx.values/speed, self.vy.values/speed # Each boid's heading
        _, _, dist = self.offsets()
        sees = dist < self.pars.radius # Including itself
        self.results.aligned[self.ti] = (np.hypot(sees @ hx, sees @ hy)/sees.sum(axis=1)).mean()
        return
```

## R

```r
boid_offsets <- function(x, y) { # The offsets from each boid to every other, the short way round the edges, and the distances
  dx <- outer(x, x, function(a, b) b - a)
  dy <- outer(y, y, function(a, b) b - a)
  dx <- dx - round(dx)
  dy <- dy - round(dy)
  list(dx = dx, dy = dy, dist = sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2))
}

Boids <- Class("Boids", ss$Module, # Flocking: each boid steers towards the heading and center of the boids it can see, and away from those too close
  radius     = par(0.1),   # How far a boid can see (the world is a unit square)
  too_close  = par(0.03),  # How close is too close
  alignment  = par(0.1),   # How strongly a boid steers towards its neighbors' heading
  cohesion   = par(0.005), # ... towards its neighbors' center
  separation = par(3e-5),  # ... away from those too close
  speed      = par(c(0.005, 0.01)), # The minimum and maximum distance moved in a step
  x  = ss$FloatArr(default = ss$random(), label = "Position (x)"),
  y  = ss$FloatArr(default = ss$random(), label = "Position (y)"),
  vx = ss$FloatArr(default = ss$uniform(-0.01, 0.01), label = "Velocity (x)"),
  vy = ss$FloatArr(default = ss$uniform(-0.01, 0.01), label = "Velocity (y)"),

  init_results = function(self) {
    ss$Module$init_results(self)
    self$define_results(ss$Result("aligned", label = "Alignment with neighbors", kind = "ratio"))
  },

  snapshot = function(self) { # A copy of the boids' positions and velocities
    list(x = py_to_r(self$x$values), y = py_to_r(self$y$values), vx = py_to_r(self$vx$values), vy = py_to_r(self$vy$values))
  },

  step = function(self) {
    p <- py_to_r(self$pars)
    x <- py_to_r(self$x$values)
    y <- py_to_r(self$y$values)
    vx <- py_to_r(self$vx$values)
    vy <- py_to_r(self$vy$values)
    o <- boid_offsets(x, y)
    dist <- o$dist
    diag(dist) <- Inf # A boid is not its own neighbor
    near <- dist < p$radius
    n_near <- pmax(rowSums(near), 1)
    close <- dist < p$too_close

    # The three rules, for all the boids at once
    steer_x <- p$alignment * (as.vector(near %*% vx) / n_near - vx) + p$cohesion * rowSums(near * o$dx) / n_near - p$separation * rowSums(close * o$dx / dist^2)
    steer_y <- p$alignment * (as.vector(near %*% vy) / n_near - vy) + p$cohesion * rowSums(near * o$dy) / n_near - p$separation * rowSums(close * o$dy / dist^2)
    alone <- rowSums(near) == 0 # A boid that sees nobody flies straight on
    vx <- vx + ifelse(alone, 0, steer_x)
    vy <- vy + ifelse(alone, 0, steer_y)

    # Keep the speed within limits, then move, wrapping around the edges
    speed <- sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2)
    factor <- pmin(pmax(speed, p$speed[1]), p$speed[2]) / speed
    self$vx[] <- vx * factor
    self$vy[] <- vy * factor
    self$x[] <- (x + vx * factor) %% 1
    self$y[] <- (y + vy * factor) %% 1
  },

  record_states = function(self) { # The state at the start of each step
    ss$Module$record_states(self)
    vx <- py_to_r(self$vx$values)
    vy <- py_to_r(self$vy$values)
    speed <- sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2)
    hx <- vx / speed # Each boid's heading
    hy <- vy / speed
    sees <- boid_offsets(py_to_r(self$x$values), py_to_r(self$y$values))$dist < py_to_r(self$pars$radius) # Including itself
    self$results$aligned[self$ti] <- mean(sqrt(as.vector(sees %*% hx)^2 + as.vector(sees %*% hy)^2) / rowSums(sees))
  }
)
```
:::

The rule of alignment is what makes a flock: without it, boids still gather and keep their distance, but each flies its own way. Here 200 boids fly for 200 steps, with and without it:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
scenarios = {
    'Flocking': ss.Sim(Boids(), n_agents=200, stop=200),
    'No alignment': ss.Sim(Boids(alignment=0), n_agents=200, stop=200),
}
msim = ss.parallel(scenarios)
msim.plot('boids.aligned')
```

## R

```r
scenarios <- list(
  "Flocking"     = Sim(Boids(), n_agents = 200, stop = 200),
  "No alignment" = Sim(Boids(alignment = 0), n_agents = 200, stop = 200)
)
msim <- parallel(scenarios) # One after another in this R session, since the boids' methods are R functions
msim$plot("boids.aligned")
```
:::

With alignment, most boids are moving with their neighbors within about 50 steps, and nearly all within 100; without it, their headings stay about as random as at the start.

The positions and velocities are states, so the flock can be drawn at any point in a run. Here the sim runs in stages (`run(until=...)` runs up to a given step, and the next call carries on from there), keeping the boids' positions and headings every 3 steps, and then plays them back as an animation, with each boid as an arrow along its heading:

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Python

```{python}
from matplotlib import animation
from IPython.display import HTML

sim = ss.Sim(Boids(), n_agents=200, stop=200, verbose=0) # Quiet: run in many stages, each would print its progress
sim.init()
boids = sim.custom.boids # A module of no standard kind, kept in sim.custom: any module that is not a disease, network, demographic module, intervention, analyzer, or connector
frames = []
for step in range(0, 201, 3):
    sim.run(until=step)
    frames.append(boids.snapshot())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 4), dpi=72)
ax.set(xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1), xticks=[], yticks=[], aspect='equal')
f = frames[0]
arrows = ax.quiver(f.x, f.y, f.vx, f.vy, angles='xy', scale_units='xy', scale=0.25, width=0.005, pivot='mid')

def draw(i):
    f = frames[i]
    arrows.set_offsets(np.c_[f.x, f.y])
    arrows.set_UVC(f.vx, f.vy)
    ax.set_title(f'Step {3*i}')

anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, draw, frames=len(frames), interval=100)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(anim.to_jshtml(default_mode='loop'))
```

## R

```r
sim <- Sim(Boids(), n_agents = 200, stop = 200, verbose = 0) # Quiet: run in many stages, each would print its progress
sim$init()
boids <- sim$custom$boids # A module of no standard kind, kept in sim$custom
frames <- list()
for (step in c(0, 30, 90, 200)) { # A few frames, side by side (for an animation, draw every few steps into a GIF, e.g. with the gifski package)
  sim$run(until = step)
  frames[[paste("Step", step)]] <- boids$snapshot()
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
for (label in names(frames)) {
  f <- frames[[label]]
  plot(f$x, f$y, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), asp = 1, xaxt = "n", yaxt = "n", xlab = "", ylab = "", main = label)
  arrows(f$x - 2 * f$vx, f$y - 2 * f$vy, f$x + 2 * f$vx, f$y + 2 * f$vy, length = 0.03) # Each boid as an arrow along its heading
}
```
:::

From random headings at the start, groups form within a few dozen steps, and by the end the boids fly as a few large flocks (which wrap around the edges of the square), with space between their members.

As in the wealth model, each rule is applied to every boid at once, as operations on arrays, rather than by looping over the boids. Working out the distance between every pair of boids takes time and memory in proportion to the square of their number, which is fine for hundreds or a few thousand; for many more, a spatial index (such as SciPy's `cKDTree`) would find each boid's neighbors faster.

## Going further

- [Custom modules](../user_guide/building_modules.qmd) covers modules written as code, with states, results, and a `step()` of their own; [T8 – Custom modules](../tutorials/t8_modules.qmd) teaches writing them.
- [Mesa: creating your first model](https://mesa.readthedocs.io/latest/tutorials/0_first_model.html): the wealth model, written in Mesa
- [Vivarium: boids](https://vivarium.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/boids.html): the boids model, in another population simulation framework
- [Boids (Reynolds)](https://www.red3d.com/cwr/boids/): the original description of the three rules of flocking
- [NetLogo: flocking model](https://ccl.northwestern.edu/netlogo/models/Flocking): flocking in NetLogo, to run and change in a browser
- [NetLogo: wealth distribution model](https://ccl.northwestern.edu/netlogo/models/WealthDistribution): a related model of how wealth becomes unequal
